extracted.intended_audience: anthology editors, short-story editors, and short-story writers (mid-20th-century literary context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for compiling an annual anthology of short fiction: standards and selection principles emphasizing memorable characterization, literary distinction, thematic balance, and editorial humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: People should come alive (vivid characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories remembered most are those in which people come alive rather than the moral or political points they make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stories that create vivid, living characters (examples cited: Naomi and Ruth, Ichabod Crane, Rip Van Winkle). Avoid selecting works that succeed only as moral or political illustrations rather than as character-driven pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize 'good, interesting writing'
rubrics_metrics.description: The over-all intent of stressing good, interesting writing has been achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary selection criterion is writing that engages the reader — interesting, well-crafted prose — rather than topicality or novelty alone. The editor explicitly says the series aims to stress 'good, interesting writing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didacticism and 'religiosity' (authentic treatment of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much religion that has been prominent in magazine fiction the past year should be called religiosity because of its artificial nature. What religion there is in Mr. Coogan’s story falls naturally into place as an important part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select religious material only when it integrates naturally into the narrative; avoid artificial or preachy religious treatments that feel like props or affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary distinction in love stories (avoid superficial 'slick' romance)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the rarest kinds of writing in America in recent years is a love story with literary distinction. The slick magazines publish many stories supposed to be about love but are mainly props for illustrations of beautiful girls and handsome men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give preference to love stories that have genuine literary merit and depth rather than those that use romance as surface glamour or illustration. Examples of acceptable love stories in this volume: 'Country Husband' (Cheever), 'The Day of the Equinox' (Curley), 'Maiden in a Tower' (Stegner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor multi-dimensional stories (richness of dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For this is a remarkable story of many dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stories that operate on multiple levels — thematic, emotional, stylistic — rather than one-dimensional pieces. The editor praises works that reveal complexity and layered meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for representative variety (avoid narrow thematic concentration)
rubrics_metrics.description: An entire collection representing American short stories for a whole year should not be limited to only children or aged characters; a representative collection should show range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to accidental biases (e.g., a first draft composed mostly of stories about the very young or very old). Re-check selections to ensure diversity of character types, ages, and subjects so the anthology reflects broader trends and avoids overconcentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial humility and awareness of temporal taste
rubrics_metrics.description: I often wish, personally, the word 'Best' were not in the title. For what is 'best' at one time will not seem so at another. More than anyone else, critics of writing and editors must be humble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the provisional and temporal nature of selections; be modest about claims of 'best.' Selection choices should be made with awareness that judgments change over time (examples: Shelley, Melville, Shakespeare's performance history).

rubrics_metrics.name: The short story as an intimate writer–reader act
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories should be read instead of talked about. Since the invention of the printing press, it has become more like the act of love. It takes place between two people, the writer and the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that create a direct, intimate connection between author and reader. This quality — an ability to be 'read' and to affect an individual reader — is a central value in selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful, iterative selection process (re-reading and self-checking)
rubrics_metrics.description: As I compiled this year’s list of contents I have worried more than usual and done much more rereading than ever before. To be frank, there really have been two lists of selections for this year’s book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated rereading and comparison to catch pattern biases and to refine the list. If an initial list skews toward a narrow theme, re-evaluate and produce alternative lists to ensure balance and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selection based on avoidance of difficult contemporary adults
rubrics_metrics.description: The only conclusion I can come to is that the modern adult exhibits a frightening complexity of traits caught in a web of appalling circumstances. The very young and the very old are usually harmless. Writers and editors both would like to avoid the kind of adult we have today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let a discomfort with complex or 'frightening' adult characters drive selection toward safer subjects (children/aged). Challenge avoidance tendencies and include works that confront complicated adult realities when they are well-written.
